title: Choosing a Name for Your Computer
summary: A republished Communications of the ACM article offering guidelines on what to do and what not to do when naming your computer. It is FYI 5 and informational.

eli5.summary: Tips on picking a good name for your computer, and what names to avoid.

subtitle: Practical advice on picking a computer name that will not confuse people, mailers or you later.

tldr.problem: Computers need names so people and software can tell them apart, but it is as easy to choose a bad name as a good one.
tldr.mechanism: The essay lists things not to do (overloaded words, your own name, long names, odd spellings, domain-like names, leading digits, odd characters) and things that work (rare words, themes, real words).
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational FYI document, a republished magazine article with no standards in it, offering lessons from experience.

sections.title: Why Names Matter
sections.content:
RFC 1178 is FYI 5, a republication of a Communications of the ACM article. It does not specify any standard. Once you have more than one computer you need to tell them apart, both in conversation ("Hey Ken. Goon is down!") and for software (mail libes@goon).

The essay is only about choosing a good name, not about how names get resolved, and it assumes the reader basically understands the domain name system from RFC 1034. A good name avoids problems people stumble over again and again.
sections.eli5: If you have two pets, you need two different names so you can call the right one. Computers are the same.

sections.title: What Not to Do
sections.content:
The first group of guidelines is about confusion in human conversation.

  • Do not overload common terms. A machine named up led to exchanges like "Is up down?".
  • Do not name it after a project unique to that machine. A machine called shop stopped fitting when more machines arrived. Numbering such as shop2 only distinguishes by number, which is fine only for many machines no human needs to tell apart.
  • Do not use your own name. It is ambiguous ("give the disk drive to don"), and a later change of machine leaves the name stuck to someone else.
  • Do not use long names. Experience shows names longer than eight characters annoy people.
  • Avoid alternate spellings. A machine called czek was mistaken for check, and pythagoris forced an administrator to look up the spelling during an outage.
  • Do not use antagonistic or embarrassing names. They distract people during demos.
sections.eli5: Do not give your computer a name that is already a normal word, your own name, or a silly spelling, because people will get mixed up when they talk about it.

sections.title: Technical Pitfalls
sections.content:
Some guidelines are technical. Avoid domain names: resolvers check non-absolute names against domains before hostnames, and some mailers refuse to treat single-token names as domains. Mail to libes@rutgers sent from yale.edu might go to rutgers.edu or rutgers.yale.edu, depending on the implementation.

Avoid domain-like names. Organizational (cia.gov) or geographical (dallas.tx.us) style names imply a connection, such as a location. Amorphous names like rivers or mythological places work fine, and "earth" is not yet a domain name.

Do not use digits at the beginning of the name. Some programs cannot tell a name from a numeric Internet address, and names made entirely of hexadecimal digits, such as beef, are also problematic. Do not use non-alphanumeric characters, because conventions on them are surprisingly nonstandard across heterogeneous networks. Do not expect case to be preserved: much software treats upper and lower case alike, and convention is all lowercase.
sections.eli5: Some computer programs get confused by names that look like numbers, have strange symbols, or look like website addresses, so keep names plain.

sections.title: What Works Well
sections.content:
The essay then gives positive advice. Use rare words such as lurch or squire rather than ones likely to arise in conversation, and prefer something like sphinx over jose, which clashes if you hire a Jose. Use theme names for groups of machines, for example colors, which will never run out, unlike finite sets such as the seven dwarfs. Other themes suggested include mythical places, elements, flowers and collectives.

Use real words: random strings are hard to remember. Do not worry about reusing someone else's hostname, except extremely well-known ones such as sri-nic and uunet. A single-part hostname is assumed to belong to the local domain, much as phone numbers are qualified by an area code when dialed from elsewhere.

The last guideline says there is always room for an exception. The author warns that renaming a machine later brings unexpected pain: obscure software refers to the old name, correspondents must be told, and old backup labels no longer match.
sections.eli5: Pick a fun group theme like colors or flowers, use real words people can remember, and choose carefully, because changing a name later is a big hassle.

references.text: Libes, D., "Choosing a Name for Your Computer", Communications of the ACM, Vol. 32, No. 11, Pg. 1289, November 1989.
Mockapetris, P., "Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities", RFC 1034, USC/Information Sciences Institute, November 1987.
